name: nc
one_line: Open a plain TCP (or UDP) connection and pipe text or files through it: the Swiss army knife for talking to services.
plain: Open a plain TCP (or UDP) connection and pipe text or files through it: the Swiss army knife for talking to services.
The sections below show when to use it, real examples, and the options explained in plain English.
when: Connect to a CTF service and read its prompt (`nc host port`).
Check whether a port is open; grab a banner; send a hand-written HTTP request.
Move a file between two machines in a lab.

examples.title: Send a message to a listener
examples.cmd: (nc -l 127.0.0.1 9099 > got.txt &) ; sleep 0.5; echo 'hello from the client' | nc -N 127.0.0.1 9099; sleep 0.5; cat got.txt

examples.title: Transfer a file and verify it
examples.cmd: (nc -l 127.0.0.1 9100 > recv.bin &) ; sleep 0.5; nc -N 127.0.0.1 9100 < hello; sleep 0.5; cmp hello recv.bin && echo identical; sha256sum hello recv.bin

options.plain: Listen for an incoming connection (OpenBSD: `nc -l HOST PORT`)
options.use: Receive a file, catch a connection in a lab

options.plain: Shut down the network socket on end of input (OpenBSD)

mistakes: There are several netcats: OpenBSD (`nc -l host port`), traditional (`nc -l -p port`, has `-e`), and `ncat` from Nmap. Check `nc -h`.
A connection that hangs often means you did not send the newline the service waits for.
Without `-N`/`-q`, a transfer may never exit; add a timeout (`-w`).
Only connect to hosts you are allowed to test.
try: Connect to the lab server and send a PUT with a body using only `nc`.
Send `hello` over UDP between two terminals (`-u`).
Check which of ports 8095-8100 are open with `nc -zv`.
